Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I have failed in my most important role in life
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, dogs as a trigger is possible but, in the absence of any related memory content, threat theme, or appraisal linking animals to the event, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the profile and is hard to integrate clinically with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal that something about the patient made the event happen is difficult to reconcile with terrorism trauma, which is typically externally caused and indiscriminate. Self-blame can occur, but this specific intrinsic-causation item is not well supported by the rest of the profile and is clinically hard to explain here.

vignette:
Elena is seventy-eight, and her world has shrunk to the size of her small apartment and the headset she wears for eight hours a day. It has been three years since the bombing at the Plaza de las Flores, three years since she lost her husband, Ricardo. She took the call center job to fill the silence, but often the voices of strangers only bring the noise rushing back. Last Tuesday, a caller, a young man, was distraught over the recent death of his father. As he spoke of the funeral, Elena felt a familiar pressure build behind her eyes. It wasn't a story that came to her, but a storm of sensations: the deafening crack that wasn't thunder, the smell of dust and something metallic, the impossible weight of Ricardo's silence next to her. The memory has no words, only a series of brutal, disjointed images she can never quite assemble. Overwhelmed by this sensory flood, she felt a wave of profound helplessness wash over her; she was certain that she was fundamentally incapable of preventing terrible things from happening, then or now.

This certainty governs her life. The moment a trigger appears-a story of loss on the phone, a sudden twinge in the vertebrae of her neck from the old injury-her first instinct is to withdraw. The conversation with the grieving young man prompted her to immediately invent a technical issue to end the call. That evening, when her daughter called to arrange a visit with the grandchildren, Elena claimed she was feeling unwell. This retreat into solitude has become her primary strategy for survival. She believes that by avoiding any deep emotional connection, she can prevent the pain of another potential loss. But this constant avoidance only deepens her conviction that she has failed in her most important role. She was a wife, and now she is a grandmother, yet she feels she is failing at both-failing to properly honor her husband's memory and failing to offer her family the warmth of a matriarch.

Her attempts to keep the memory at bay have paradoxically given it more power. She refuses to talk about that day, and her family, respecting her pain, has learned not to ask. She takes a bus route that adds forty minutes to her commute just to avoid passing anywhere near the rebuilt plaza. She dreads the anniversary, a day she spends with the phone unplugged and the curtains drawn. This careful avoidance has cemented the memory in its pre-verbal state; it remains a terrifying collage of sensory fragments, forever unprocessed. The gaps in her recollection-the minutes just before and after the blast-are not empty spaces but black holes of self-blame. The fact that she cannot construct a linear story feels like a profound personal failing, proof that she is broken beyond repair. This wordless, fractured memory constantly reinforces her belief that her life is over, that there is no future beyond this cycle of fear and remembrance.

The cycle is relentlessly self-sustaining. The memory itself has become a trigger. Sometimes, for no reason at all, a flash of the memory-the feeling of being thrown, the sharp impact-will surface, and the chronic pain in her neck will flare into an acute, searing ache. This physical pain then acts as a potent reminder of the event, pulling the other sensory fragments along with it, which in turn reinforces her feelings of hopelessness and her need to withdraw further. The more she isolates herself to manage these episodes, the more the memories fester, unshared and unexamined. Her avoidance has become a cage, built to protect her, but it has only served to lock her in with the very things she fears most.

It was her granddaughter, Sofia, who finally broke through. After weeks of unanswered calls, the ten-year-old showed up at the door alone, holding a drawing of the two of them. "Abuela," she had asked, her voice small, "why don't you want to see me anymore?" Seeing the hurt in her eyes, Elena felt the full weight of her self-imposed isolation. It was one thing to believe she had failed Ricardo, but to see the tangible proof of her failure as a grandmother standing before her was unbearable. She has come to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that the memories will consume her, but even more terrified of losing what little connection she has left.
